docs.title: MMDBBench
docs.text:
MMDBBench is an open benchmark of multi-model databases: databases that serve tables, time series, documents, graphs, key-values, and vectors from one storage engine. Specialist databases built for a single model run the same tasks as per-model baselines, so a reader can see what one engine gives up or gains against the engine built for that job. Tasks are written in SQL, Cypher, and each engine's native language, and run on x86 Linux. MMDBBench runs the same tasks on the same machine with published settings, records every result with the exact engine version that produced it, and keeps the history, so a number can always be traced and a change can always be seen.

Status

The protocol version is 2026-11, in development until its first release; the first published results will be measured with it. The benchmark code is still developed in humemai/arcadedb-embedded-python (benchmarks/) and moves into this repository after its first paper. The live results are on the project page; these documents describe how they are produced.

docs.title: Lanes
docs.text:
lane what it measures Tables documents and SQL analytics Graphs interactive queries and analytical queries over a social graph Vectors dense and sparse similarity search Time series ingestion and the usual monitoring queries Cross-model queries that combine more than one data model in one transaction Lifecycle durability, restarts and the cost of staying consistent

Every engine is compared only in the lanes it is built for. An in-process engine and a server engine are different categories and are labelled as such.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: Changes to the protocol, newest first. Engine versions are not listed here; they are on every result row.

docs.title: 2026-11 (in development)
docs.text:
The benchmark was renamed from DBBench to MMDBBench on 2026-11-07 and refocused on multi-model databases. The protocol version is unchanged.

The protocol version, in development until its first release. The method is described on the Methodology page.

Method changes made while it is in development, before any result is published with them:

  • Served ArcadeDB leaves the initial heap (-Xms) unset, like embedded ArcadeDB. Neo4j and Elasticsearch keep a pinned initial heap, as their vendors recommend.
  • Neo4j's heap and page cache come from its own neo4j-admin server memory-recommendation for each memory cap. Elasticsearch's heap is the smaller of the tier heap, 50% of the cap and 26 GiB.
  • Container io figures count a stacked block device once. Earlier rows summed every device line of the cgroup io.stat, which counted the benchmark machine's NVMe disk and the device-mapper device on top of it twice. The harness now stamps io_stat_dedup: 1 into each row, and the frozen table halves the io figures of rows without the stamp (see Result rows).
  • Milvus runs as 3.0.3 on the vendor's Docker Compose standalone (three containers sharing the cell's memory cap), ingests by bulk import, waits for every segment to be flushed and the index to be finished before timed searches, and records the storage mode, the output fields and the filter. Storage V3 is a sensitivity setting.
A development release, superseded by 2026-11 before any comparison was published from it.

docs.title: Tell us a setting is wrong
docs.text:
Open an issue on humemai/mmdbbench with:

  • the engine and the version it applies to,
  • the setting we use and the setting you recommend for this task,
  • where your documentation says so.

We re-run the affected cells with your configuration on the same machine and publish them beside the earlier result, with the reason. The earlier result stays in the history.

docs.title: Add an engine, a query or a lane
docs.text: Open an issue first describing the task and the engine's recommended setup. A new engine joins a lane when it can run the lane's full task list or when its gaps are declared.

docs.title: Report a problem with a result
docs.text: Include the cell (lane, scale, workload, engine, version) and what you expected. If the answer digest differs from the one you get, say so: that is the most useful kind of report.

docs.title: Engines
docs.text:
Generated page

This page is generated from the result rows and the override registry, and is not edited by hand. It is empty until the first 2026-11 rows land.

For every engine in every lane, this page will state what we run: the version, the container image digest where a row records one, the durability classes measured, the tiers, every setting a row carries, and each override of an engine's default with the reason. Everything will be read from the result rows and the override registry, so it cannot drift from what was measured. The rules these settings follow are on the Methodology page.

No row has been measured with the 2026-11 instrument yet, so there is nothing to list. The page is generated by benchmarks/experiments/gen_engines_doc.py in humemai/arcadedb-embedded-python from the clean rows of the 2026-11 instrument (the newest clean row of each cell, on the serial CPU set), together with the failed cells, which are listed as the result they are. It replaces this text when the first 2026-11 rows land. The earlier 2026-10 instrument was a development version; its rows were never published as a comparison and are not shown.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: These are the rules every published result follows. A result that breaks one of them is not published as a comparison; it is published as a declared exception, or not at all.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
1. Same task, same data, same machine. Every engine in a lane answers the same queries over the same corpus on the same dedicated machine. The machine's specification is on the results page.
  2. Answers are checked. Each query's answer is reduced to a digest and compared between engines. A fast wrong answer is a failure, not a result.
  3. Settings are published. Each engine runs at its documented defaults unless a setting is required to run the task (a memory limit, a durability class, an index the task needs). Every deviation is listed on the Engines page with the reason. An index added for one engine is added, in its equivalent form, for every engine that has one.
  4. Equal resources. Every engine gets the same memory cap and CPU allotment inside a lane, and the same durability classes are measured for every engine that offers them (a relaxed class and a strict class where the engine supports both).
  5. Repetitions and medians. Each cell is run up to five times, in whole passes of one repetition each: three repetitions for every engine first (the four ArcadeDB arms included), then a fourth, then a fifth. The page prints the median with the minimum and maximum, never a single run and never the mean, and states the number of repetitions behind a table whenever it is below five.
  6. Budgets and censoring. A query that cannot finish within its time budget is recorded as censored, with the budget, and is never silently dropped or counted as fast. Where an engine can be asked to stop a query itself, the budget is enforced by the engine; otherwise it is checked between iterations.
  7. Failures are results. An engine that runs out of memory, times out or refuses a task has that recorded as its result for the cell, with the error it gave.
  8. Versions are exact. Every row records the engine version and, for containers, the image digest it ran on. A cell never mixes rows from different versions: when an engine ships a new version, new rows are added next to the old ones. ArcadeDB is pinned by upstream commit rather than by release number when it runs a development build, because its build line reads the same development version for every commit; its embedded and server arms in one table are built from the same commit and run the same JVM. The 2026-11 measurement of ArcadeDB runs the 26.11.1 release in four arms: embedded and served, each on the JVM and as the native build.
  9. Warm-up is declared. Whether a timing includes the first run, a warm-up, or an index build is stated in the table it appears in.
  10. History is kept. A correction or a new version adds rows; the earlier rows stay visible.

docs.title: The 2026-11 instrument
docs.text:
The protocol version is 2026-11, in development until its first release, and every row is stamped with the instrument that measured it. There is one method and no switch for another: the harness refuses to run a cell under any other instrument value. These choices are part of the instrument and are the same for every cell:

  • A warm-up before the sparse search. Every sparse engine runs 1,000 untimed searches on queries that are not in the timed set, so a query or result cache cannot flatter an engine.
  • The CPU idle state is held for each timed cell, at the lowest latency target, so a single-client time under a millisecond does not include a core waking up. A cell that cannot take the hold still runs, and the row says so.
  • The dense lane indexes the vector id on every engine that would otherwise scan for the record it deletes, so the delete column compares indexed lookups.
  • Each JVM engine runs the memory settings its vendor documents. The memory cap is the same for every engine in a cell. The heap inside it is not one Java rule for all: ArcadeDB, embedded and served, sets only -Xmx (the tier heap) and leaves the initial heap unset; Neo4j and Elasticsearch pin the initial heap to the maximum, as their documentation recommends, and take the heap their vendors' rules give for the cap. The table below lists the setting, the vendor's sentence and what the memory column shows for each engine.
  • Milvus runs as its vendor ships it. Milvus 3.0.3 runs as the vendor's Docker Compose standalone: Milvus, etcd and MinIO as three containers, every image pinned by digest. Data goes in by Milvus's bulk import, not by insert batches. Storage V2, Milvus's default, is the headline; Storage V3 is a switch used only for a sensitivity run, and every row records the mode it ran in. Details are in Milvus.
  • Served ArcadeDB is measured with the vendor's official Python driver as the headline, and the same cell runs again on the lean HTTP client of the harness as a labelled sensitivity row. Bulk loads and transactions stay on the lean client.
  • Large results are read on each engine's documented bulk path (Arrow for embedded ArcadeDB and DuckDB), with the plain-Python read timed beside it. Small results do not move. The typed read must return the same answer as the plain read, or the cell ends.
  • Memory, disk and IO are read at the end of every phase of a cell (load, index build, warm-up, queries, and idle), between two timed sections and never inside one. The headline memory is the memory the cell's containers own, the same kernel counter for every engine, summed over every container of a multi-container deployment; the heap figures of JVM engines are context and are not compared across engines. Disk and IO are read the same way for every engine.
  • The dense lane compares engines at matched recall. After the build, the lane runs one timed pass per search-beam value on the same index (ef of 50, 100, 200 and 400 for the HNSW engines; ArangoDB's nProbe at 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 times its calibrated value). The headline is the lowest median latency among the passes whose recall@10 reaches 0.95, with the beam that won it. An engine that never reaches 0.95 is printed as not reached with its best recall, never as a slower or lower-recall number. Engines with no beam setting run one pass.
  • Product-quantization (PQ) arms are off for now. They run beside the full-precision and int8 arms only when enabled, with the same setting for every engine that offers it: 32 subspaces of 256 centroids, and a re-rank of the stored vectors where the engine can do one. They stay off until the measured ArcadeDB release carries the upstream PQ fixes (ArcadeData/arcadedb#10516 to #10519), because before them ArcadeDB's SQL search ignores a PQ index and would measure exact search under a PQ label.

The harness documents these choices in PROTOCOL.md and FAIRNESS.md. The 2026-10 instrument was a development version and is retired: nothing is measured with it again, and no result from it is published.

docs.title: JVM and memory settings per engine
docs.text:
Every engine runs the memory configuration its own vendor recommends, and every engine gets the same memory cap. A pinned initial heap (-Xms equal to -Xmx) makes the JVM commit the whole heap at start, so the kernel's memory counters read toward the cap whatever the engine needs. That is the cost of the vendor's recommended setup, and it is reported as such. The heap figures of a JVM engine (used after a full collection, committed) are recorded on the row beside the headline as context and are not compared across engines.

Engine Heap setting the harness passes Initial heap Vendor source What the memory column shows ArcadeDB embedded -Xmx of the tier heap, through the bindings' heap_size not pinned The Python bindings' documented practice; ArcadeDB's maintainers advise no -Xms in a container with a fixed memory budget (ArcadeData/arcadedb#9167, arcadedb-docs "JVM settings in a fixed memory budget"). demand, up to -Xmx ArcadeDB served ARCADEDB_OPTS_MEMORY=-Xmx{heap}, the tier heap not pinned The same guidance, so embedded and served ArcadeDB run one JVM configuration and the comparison isolates transport. demand, up to -Xmx Neo4j server.memory.heap.initial_size = server.memory.heap.max_size, the heap that neo4j-admin server memory-recommendation prints for the cap (next table) pinned Neo4j memory configuration: "It is recommended to set these two parameters to the same value to avoid unwanted full garbage collection pauses." reads toward the cap Elasticsearch ES_JAVA_OPTS=-Xms{heap} -Xmx{heap}; the heap is the smaller of the tier heap, 50% of the cap and 26 GiB pinned Elasticsearch advanced configuration: "The minimum and maximum values must be the same." and "Set Xms and Xmx to no more than 50% of the total memory available to each Elasticsearch node." reads toward the cap QuestDB none: the image's own defaults the image's The QuestDB configuration page has no JVM heap recommendation, so the harness sets none. the image's own JVM behaviour; the row records the tier heap although no heap reaches the server

An unpinned heap is no cure for the headline either: a JVM that has grown stays grown unless the collector returns the pages, which is why the used-after-collection figure sits beside it.

docs.title: Neo4j heap and page cache
docs.text:
Neo4j's manual says: "Use the neo4j-admin server memory-recommendation command to get an initial recommendation." The harness runs that command from the pinned Neo4j image for each memory cap in the benchmark's tier table, on an empty data directory, and uses what it prints as the heap (initial equal to maximum) and the page cache. The tool's raw output is kept in the harness repository and a test holds the table in the code equal to it.

Memory cap Heap Page cache 8g 3600m 2g 12g 4600m 4g 16g 5g 7g 24g 8g 10g 28g 10g 11g 32g 12g 12g 36g 13800m 14g 48g 18g 20g

The tool also prints -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError; the harness does not set it. The tool computes the page cache for an empty data directory, so it does not account for the size of the loaded database.

docs.title: Elasticsearch heap
docs.text: Elastic recommends a heap of no more than 50% of the node's memory and below the threshold for compressed object pointers: "The exact threshold varies but 26GB is safe on most systems and can be as large as 30GB on some systems." The harness takes the smaller of the tier heap, 50% of the cap and 26 GiB, with the initial and maximum heap equal. The rule can only lower a heap; on a tier whose heap is already at most half the cap and under 26 GiB it changes nothing.

docs.title: ArcadeDB page cache
docs.text: arcadedb.maxPageRAM is not set, so the engine's default applies, a quarter of -Xmx, on both deployments.

docs.title: Milvus
docs.text:
• Deployment. Milvus 3.0.3 as in the vendor's milvus-standalone-docker-compose.yaml: Milvus, etcd (v3.5.25) and MinIO (milvusdb/minio, RELEASE.2024-12-18T13-15-44Z) as three containers, each pinned by its amd64 manifest digest (Milvus 812cb91a, etcd dc2bdc58, MinIO 34c8e2f5; the row records the full digests). The runner starts the three containers itself, in the cell's CPU set and network, and removes them after the cell; it does not call docker compose. The client is pymilvus 3.0.2 with the bulk_writer extra. Every setting not named here is the compose default, and no configuration file is mounted. The dense arms raise dataCoord.segment.sealProportion from 0.12 to 0.5 through an environment variable, so a 10M ingest lands in the merged segment layout directly.
  • Storage mode. Storage V2, Milvus's default, is the headline. Storage V3 (common.storage.useLoonFFI=true) is one switch for a sensitivity run, written to its own results file, and every row records the mode it ran in.
  • Ingest. Milvus's bulk import: Parquet written through RemoteBulkWriter into Milvus's own MinIO, then one import job. File preparation, upload and the job are all inside the ingest time and are also recorded apart. The sparse and the dense lane use the same path, as pgvector uses COPY and Elasticsearch its bulk helper.
  • Before any timed search. The runner waits until every segment is Flushed, the index is Finished with nothing pending, and the loaded segments hold every row. The seal wait, the index wait and the load are each timed on their own and recorded on the row.
  • What a search returns. Ids and distances only: no output fields, no vector field and no filter. The row records the output fields and the filter, both empty.
  • Memory. The three containers share the cell's one memory cap, as every other engine's server side has it. etcd takes 512m and MinIO 1g out of the cap, the Milvus container gets the rest, and the split is recorded on the row. The row's memory, CPU, I/O and disk figures are the three containers added together.
  • Index parameters. HNSW M 16, efConstruction 100 and ef 100, the HNSW_SQ SQ8 arm, and the sparse inverted index are unchanged. Equal ef is not equal recall, so every row carries recall@10 beside latency, and the dense lane's beam sweep reports latency at matched recall.

docs.title: Reading a result
docs.text: A bar or a number is only meaningful with its footnotes: the category (in-process or server), the durability class, the scale, the version, and whether any query in the cell was censored. The results page carries all of these next to every number.

docs.title: What this benchmark does not claim
docs.text: It does not rank databases in general. It measures the tasks listed in each lane on the stated machine and settings. A different workload, scale or tuning can change the order, which is why the settings are published and why vendors are asked to review them.

docs.title: Related work
docs.text:
Four academic benchmarks already address multi-model databases.

  • UniBench, from the University of Helsinki: relational, JSON, XML, key-value, and graph data in one social commerce scenario, with multi-model queries and transactions.
  • M2Bench, from Seoul National University: analytic tasks over relational, document, property graph, and array data, run on polyglot persistence (MySQL, MongoDB, Neo4j, and SciDB), ArangoDB, and AgensGraph.
  • MMSBench-Net, from the University of Basel: a scenario-based benchmark over relational, document, and graph data, used to compare Polypheny and SurrealDB.
  • GRBench, by Liu and colleagues: relational and graph data together, evaluated on relational extensions, multi-model databases, and dedicated graph-relational systems.

None of the four lists vectors or time series among its data models.

docs.title: What MMDBBench does differently
docs.text:
• It adds vectors and time series to the models a multi-model engine serves.
  • It runs a specialist database for each model as a baseline, so the question is what one engine gains or gives up against a specialist, not only how two multi-model systems compare.
  • Tasks are written in SQL, Cypher, and each engine's native language, and the answers are checked between engines.
  • It runs on one platform, x86 Linux, with pinned engine versions and published settings.
  • The raw result rows are open: see Result rows.

These descriptions come from each benchmark's own page or paper, linked above. They say what each one states about itself, not how it performs.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
Every published number can be repeated on your own hardware. The benchmark runs each engine in a container pinned by image digest (or an installed package pinned by version) and writes one result row per measurement; the tables on the results page are generated from those rows.

Status

The reproduction instructions move here with the benchmark code. Until then the code and its instructions are in humemai/arcadedb-embedded-python under benchmarks/.

A reproduction is comparable when it keeps the memory cap, the durability class and the corpus the same, and compares engines on the same machine. Absolute times on different hardware will differ; the order of engines and the size of the gaps are what a reproduction should be compared on.

docs.title: Result rows
docs.text:
One published measurement is one row. A row says what ran, on what, and how it went. The fields below are the ones every row carries; lanes add their own metrics.

field meaning backend the engine and arm that ran, for example an in-process arm or a server arm lane the lane (tables, graphs, vectors, time series, cross-model, lifecycle) scale / tier the corpus size workload the task within the lane rep the repetition number engine_version the exact engine version; container runs also record the image digest durability_class the durability class the run used, where the engine offers more than one mem_cap the memory cap the run had io_*_mib the bytes the cell's containers read from and wrote to disk, per phase and in total, from the container's io.stat. Rows written on the benchmark machine before the fix for issue #555 counted a stacked block device (an NVMe disk and the device-mapper device on top of it) twice, so those figures are about twice their value. The fixed harness counts the device once and stamps io_stat_dedup: 1 into the row; the frozen table halves the io figures of the earlier rows, which lack the stamp, and lists each corrected row with its raw values in generated/io_stat_correction.json error / oom_killed what went wrong, if anything; a failure is a result metric fields latencies (median and percentiles), throughput, peak memory and the like, per lane *_censored / *_budget_s whether a query hit its time budget, and the budget

Rows are never edited. A correction adds a row; the history keeps both. The one correction made after the fact is the io figures above, which is applied in the frozen copy the tables are built from, never in the recorded rows.
